cues.text: Six Hosts for Six Captains
On February 23, 1239, Christian forces from Daroca, Teruel, and Calatayud gathered on Mount Codol to retake the castle of Chío near Luchente from Moorish control.
The army's chaplain, Fr. Mateo Martínez , celebrated Mass and consecrated six hosts, one for each captain, before word arrived that Moorish troops were already advancing.
Hidden Among the Rocks
With no time to distribute Communion before the fighting began, Martínez wrapped the six hosts in the corporal , the linen cloth spread beneath the chalice at Mass.
He hid the bundle among the hillside rocks.
When the battle ended in a Christian victory, he retrieved it and reportedly found the cloth soaked through with blood where the hosts had rested.
A Draw the Losers Would Not Accept
Each of the six captains represented a different town of Aragon and wanted the relic carried home to his own city.
Three successive drawings of lots favored Daroca, a result two losing captains refused to accept.
The army's general then proposed a solution none of them could dispute.
The Mule's Journey
The corporals were placed on the back of a captured Moorish mule, then released to wander unguided wherever it chose.
Setting out on February 24, the animal walked more than two hundred miles before collapsing from exhaustion in Daroca’s streets on March 7, 1239.
Clergy and soldiers reportedly accompanied the journey on foot, with candles lit the whole way.
Legacy
A church dedicated to Our Lady, later rebuilt as the Basilica of Santa María de los Sagrados Corporales , was raised in Daroca to house the relic.
In 1261, a delegation traveled to Rome to report the miracle to Pope Urban IV.
Prompted partly by this and by a further Eucharistic sign at Bolsena two years later, he would establish the universal feast of Corpus Christi in 1264.
The bloodstained corporals remain enshrined at Daroca today, carried each year in a procession the city has kept, by its own reckoning, since the very year the mule first collapsed within its walls.
